parsed_answer.content:
In high-throughput concurrent Java applications, relying on traditional synchronized blocks or ReentrantLocks can introduce severe performance bottlenecks due to thread contention, context switching, and OS-level kernel transitions. Atomic classes—specifically AtomicInteger and AtomicReference—solve this problem by providing lock-free, thread-safe operations on single variables. AtomicInteger encapsulates a primitive int value, while AtomicReference manages an object reference pointer, ensuring that read-modify-write sequences execute indivisibly without blocking competing threads.

To achieve thread safety without synchronization, atomic classes bypass traditional monitor locks (synchronized) entirely. Instead, they rely on hardware-level CPU instructions, most notably Compare-And-Swap (CAS). A CAS operation takes three operands: a memory location (V), the expected old value (A), and a new value (B). The CPU atomically executes the logic: if the value at V equals A, then it updates V to B and returns true; otherwise, it does nothing and returns false. This optimistic concurrency control model allows multiple threads to attempt updates simultaneously; if a thread fails because another thread modified the variable in the interim, it simply retries in a tight spin loop until it succeeds, preventing deadlocks and reducing thread suspension overhead.

rows: Low CPU cycles, potential busy-wait loop cost

items: Under the hood, atomic classes rely heavily on sun.misc.Unsafe (or VarHandle in modern Java versions) to execute native CPU instructions like CMPXCHG on x86 architectures.

The target fields inside AtomicInteger and AtomicReference are marked with the volatile keyword, guaranteeing visibility across threads by establishing a happens-before relationship without locking memory buses unnecessarily.

CAS operations suffer from the ABA problem: if a value changes from A to B and back to A, a CAS check assumes nothing changed. This is mitigated in concurrent collections and specialized classes using version stamps like AtomicStampedReference.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of high contention scenarios: while CAS outperforms locks when thread contention is low to moderate, under extreme thread contention, the continuous spinning of dozens of CPU cores trying to update the same AtomicInteger can burn 100% CPU cycles. For high-contention accumulators, always prefer LongAdder or DoubleAdder over AtomicInteger.

title: What are Atomic classes (AtomicInteger, AtomicReference)? How do they achieve thread safety without synchronization?
